title: LAS, LAZ and E57
cards/0/body:
LAS is specified by ASPRS, the American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing. It is a binary file: a header and point records of equal size.

There are several record formats. For example, format 7 in LAS 1.4: coordinates, intensity, return number, class, GPS time and color, 36 bytes per point.
cards/0/deep: Coordinates are stored as 32-bit integers with a scale and offset from the header: X = Xrecord × scale + offset. That way millimeter precision fits in 4 bytes even for coordinates hundreds of kilometers out.
cards/1/body:
LAZ (LASzip) compresses LAS losslessly, usually down to 7–20% of the size. Decompress it and you get the original LAS, byte for byte.

That is why scan archives are almost always kept in LAZ.
cards/2/task: A 100-million-point scan has to fit into 1 GB. Pick a format in the calculator.
cards/3/q: Why did LAZ fit while LAS did not?
cards/3/options/0: LAZ compresses the same data losslessly several times over
cards/3/explain: Nothing is lost: neighboring points are similar, and the algorithm encodes the difference between them.
cards/4/body:
E57 is the ASTM E2807 standard. It stores not only points but the structure of the survey: where the scanner stood, each station’s point grid, and panoramic photos.

It is handy for exchange between software from different scanner makers.
cards/5/q: You need to hand over scans along with panoramic photos from each station. What do you pick?
cards/5/explain: LAS and XYZ store only points. E57 can hold images and station positions too.
cards/6/q: How much space do 10 million points at 36 bytes take?
cards/7/options/1: A LAS point can have a class
cards/7/explain: LAS is binary, and LAZ gives the data back byte for byte.
cards/8/pairs/2/1: Open ASTM format with scans and photos
